passages.label: Screening lab
paragraphs: A perception laboratory runs three short tasks with volunteers. In the tone task, a quiet sound starts below hearing level and slowly grows louder until the volunteer first reports hearing it. In the weight task, a volunteer holds a standard object and a slightly heavier one and says whether the two feel different. In the screening task, trained inspectors watch a fast stream of bag images and press a key whenever they spot a rare hidden blade.

The team records several patterns. Inspectors who are told that blades are common report far more blades, including in bags that are actually empty. A steady ventilation hum in the room stops being noticed after a few minutes. Adding a small weight is easier to detect when the standard object is light than when it is heavy. When the room lights are dimmed, volunteers say colors wash out but they still catch movement at the edges of their vision.

questions.stem: In the tone task, the softest sound level a volunteer can detect on about half of the trials is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: The absolute threshold is the lowest stimulus intensity a person can detect 50 percent of the time, while the difference threshold and just noticeable difference involve telling two stimuli apart.

questions.stem: Volunteers notice an added weight more easily when the standard object is light than when it is heavy. Which principle best explains this?
choices: The just noticeable difference is a roughly constant proportion of the standard stimulus
The absolute threshold falls as stimulus intensity rises
Adaptation erases any constant stimulus within seconds
Detection depends only on the observer's expectations
questions.explain: Weber's law holds that the just noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the original stimulus, so a heavier standard needs a larger absolute change before the difference is felt.

questions.stem: Inspectors told that blades are common report more blades even in empty bags. In signal detection terms, this instruction most directly shifts which of the following?
choices: Their absolute sensitivity to the visual stimulus
Their decision criterion for reporting a blade
The Weber fraction for their visual system
The rate of transduction in their retina
questions.explain: Expecting frequent targets lowers the response criterion, increasing both hits and false alarms without changing the underlying ability to see the blade.

questions.stem: The volunteers stop noticing the steady ventilation hum after a few minutes. This change is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Sensory adaptation is the decline in sensitivity to a constant, unchanging stimulus over time.

questions.stem: The tendency for expectation to make inspectors perceive blades that are not present is the clearest example of which of the following?
questions.explain: Top-down processing uses prior knowledge and expectations to interpret sensory input, which can produce perceptions that do not match the actual stimulus.

questions.stem: When the room is dimmed, colors fade but movement at the edges of vision is still detected. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Cones in the periphery specialize in dim-light motion
Rods, dense in the periphery, work in dim light but do not code color
The fovea contains only rods that detect motion
Rods encode fine color while cones handle dim light
questions.explain: Rods are concentrated in the peripheral retina and are highly sensitive in low light but do not encode color, so peripheral motion is seen while color washes out.

passages.label: Study habits study
paragraphs: A psychology class tests how study methods affect memory. Students learn a 30-item word list, then take a recall test either right away or after a delay. One group repeats the words over and over silently. A second group links each word to a personal image or story. A third group is quizzed repeatedly instead of rereading.

The results show that the story group recalls far more words than the repeating group. On the immediate test, students recall the first and last items best. A week later, several students confidently recall a related word, sofa, that was never on the list after learning words like chair, table, and couch. Students who were quizzed during learning outperform those who only reread.

questions.stem: The group that linked each word to a personal image or story remembered the most. This advantage is best explained by which of the following?
choices: Maintenance rehearsal strengthens the sensory register
Deeper, elaborative encoding creates more retrieval routes
Shorter words move faster into long-term memory
questions.explain: Elaborative encoding that connects new material to existing knowledge produces more durable memories and more cues for later retrieval than simple repetition.

questions.stem: On the immediate test, students recall the first and last words best. The strong recall of the last few words just presented is best attributed to which of the following?
choices: The primacy effect and long-term storage
The recency effect and recent items still in working memory
Deeper encoding of the final items
questions.explain: The recency effect reflects the last items still being available in short-term or working memory, while the primacy effect reflects earlier items reaching long-term storage.

questions.stem: A week later some students confidently recall the word sofa, which was never shown, after learning words like chair, table, and couch. This best illustrates which of the following?
choices: A false memory built from related, activated concepts
questions.explain: Recalling a strongly related but unpresented word reflects a false memory produced when associated concepts are activated during encoding and later mistaken for the original.

questions.stem: Students quizzed during learning later outperform those who only reread. This finding is best labeled as which of the following?
choices: The testing, or retrieval practice, effect
questions.explain: The testing effect is the finding that actively retrieving information strengthens later memory more than passive rereading.

questions.stem: One student recalls more words when tested in the same room where she studied than in a new room. This is best explained by which of the following?
questions.explain: Context-dependent memory reflects encoding specificity, where cues present at encoding, such as the room, aid retrieval when they are present again.

questions.stem: To hold a 10-digit number long enough to dial it, a student groups the digits into three clusters. Grouping helps mainly by doing which of the following?
choices: Expanding the absolute capacity of long-term memory
Reducing the number of items working memory must juggle
Converting the digits into iconic sensory memory
questions.explain: Chunking reorganizes many items into a few meaningful units, easing the limited capacity of working memory.

passages.label: Emotion study
paragraphs: Researchers study how the body and mind combine to produce emotion. In one setup, volunteers are shown a frightening film while their heart rate and sweating are recorded. In another, volunteers exercise on a bike and then meet a stranger, and researchers measure how attracted they feel.

Some volunteers are given a shot they are told is a vitamin but that actually speeds the heart. When these aroused volunteers wait with a cheerful actor, they report feeling happy; when they wait with an irritated actor, they report feeling angry. Volunteers who just exercised rate the stranger as more attractive than resting volunteers do.

questions.stem: Aroused volunteers feel happy near a cheerful actor but angry near an irritated actor. Which theory best explains this pattern?
questions.explain: The two-factor theory holds that emotion arises from physiological arousal plus a cognitive label drawn from the situation, so the same arousal is interpreted differently depending on context.

questions.stem: Volunteers who just exercised rate a stranger as more attractive than resting volunteers do. This is best explained as which of the following?
choices: Misattribution of physiological arousal to the stranger
A conditioned emotional response to exercise
questions.explain: Leftover arousal from exercise is misattributed to the stranger, increasing reported attraction, an application of two-factor emotion ideas.

questions.stem: A different theory claims the volunteers first notice their racing heart and sweating and then feel afraid because of those bodily changes. This describes which theory?
questions.explain: The James-Lange theory proposes that a physiological reaction to a stimulus comes first and the felt emotion is our reading of that bodily state.

questions.stem: Suppose data showed that the racing heart and the feeling of fear begin at the same time and independently. This finding would most support which theory?
questions.explain: The Cannon-Bard theory holds that physiological arousal and the subjective emotion occur simultaneously and independently.

questions.stem: The rapid fear response to the frightening film is most associated with activity in which brain structure?
questions.explain: The amygdala, part of the limbic system, is central to processing fear and other strong emotional responses.

questions.stem: Researchers find that people across very different cultures produce and recognize the same facial expression for disgust. This best supports which idea?
choices: Display rules fully determine facial expressions
Some basic emotional expressions are universal
Emotions are learned only through operant conditioning
Facial expressions have no link to felt emotion
questions.explain: Cross-cultural recognition of the same expressions supports the view that a set of basic emotions and their expressions are universal, consistent with work by Ekman.

passages.label: Personality clinic
paragraphs: A counseling center interviews clients and records how they describe themselves and handle conflict. One client, after being passed over for a promotion, insists the job was boring anyway and channels his frustration into intense exercise. Another completes a questionnaire that scores five broad traits.

The center also asks about beliefs. One client strongly agrees that outcomes in life come from his own actions, while another believes outcomes are mostly due to luck and powerful others. A therapist notes that a warm, accepting environment seems to help clients move toward their goals, and that one client is imaginative, curious, and eager to try new activities.

questions.stem: The client who calls the lost job boring and pours frustration into exercise is using which pair of defense mechanisms?
questions.explain: Rationalization offers a self-justifying reason (the job was boring), while sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into a socially acceptable outlet like exercise.

questions.stem: The client who believes outcomes come from his own actions rather than luck would be described as having which of the following?
questions.explain: An internal locus of control is the belief that one's own actions determine outcomes, in contrast to an external locus that credits luck or powerful others.

questions.stem: According to psychoanalytic theory, the part of personality that would push the passed-over client to lash out immediately, with no concern for consequences, is which of the following?
questions.explain: The id seeks immediate gratification of impulses without regard for reality or morality, unlike the reality-oriented ego and the moralistic superego.

questions.stem: The therapist's finding that a warm, accepting environment helps clients grow toward their goals fits most closely with which approach?
questions.explain: Humanistic theorists such as Rogers emphasize unconditional positive regard and a supportive environment as conditions for growth and self-actualization.

questions.stem: One client scores very high on a broad trait: she is imaginative, curious, and eager to try new activities. She is highest on which of the Big Five traits?
questions.explain: Openness to experience captures imagination, curiosity, and willingness to try new things.

questions.stem: Bandura's social-cognitive view differs from pure trait theory mainly because it emphasizes which of the following?
choices: The ongoing interaction of personal factors, behavior, and environment
Unconscious conflicts among id, ego, and superego
A single universal hierarchy of needs
questions.explain: Social-cognitive theory stresses reciprocal determinism, the two-way interaction among personal factors, behavior, and the environment, rather than fixed traits or unconscious drives.

passages.label: Campus experiments
paragraphs: A social psychology team runs several campus studies. In one, students solve simple problems either alone or in front of an audience. In another, students pull a rope alone or as part of a group while the team measures effort. In a third, a staged emergency, someone drops a stack of books, and researchers vary how many bystanders are present.

The team finds that experts perform simple tasks faster with an audience, while beginners do worse on hard tasks when watched. Individual effort on the rope drops as group size grows. Help for the person who dropped the books is offered quickly when one bystander is present but is delayed when many are present. In a mock jury task, small groups make riskier decisions than the members did on their own.

questions.stem: Experts complete simple tasks faster with an audience, but beginners do worse on hard tasks when watched. This overall pattern is best explained by which of the following?
choices: Social facilitation, where arousal boosts the dominant response
questions.explain: Social facilitation predicts that the arousal from an audience strengthens the dominant response, helping performance on easy or well-learned tasks and hurting it on difficult or novel ones.

questions.stem: Individual effort on the rope-pull drops as the group grows larger. This reduction in personal effort is best labeled as which of the following?
questions.explain: Social loafing is the tendency to exert less individual effort when working in a group than when working alone.

questions.stem: Help is offered quickly with one bystander but delayed when many are present. The best explanation is which of the following?
choices: Diffusion of responsibility among many bystanders
questions.explain: As the number of bystanders rises, responsibility to act is diffused across the group, so any single person feels less compelled to help.

questions.stem: In a follow-up, a student gives an obviously wrong answer to a simple line-length question after hearing several confederates give that same wrong answer. This behavior is best explained by which of the following?
choices: Informational social influence based on genuine confusion
Normative social influence to fit in with the group
questions.explain: Conforming to a clearly wrong majority on an easy task reflects normative influence, the desire to be accepted, rather than genuine uncertainty about the answer.

questions.stem: A different study asks participants to follow an experimenter's direct instructions to deliver what they believe are harmful shocks. This situation tests which of the following most directly?
questions.explain: Following the direct commands of an authority figure, even against one's conscience, is obedience, as studied by Milgram, and differs from peer conformity.

questions.stem: The mock juries make riskier decisions than the individual members did beforehand. This shift toward a more extreme group position is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Group polarization is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen the members' initial leanings, producing a more extreme collective decision.

passages.label: Clinic and classroom
paragraphs: A clinic uses learning principles to change behavior. A child learns that a soft chime always comes right before a bitter cough syrup, and after several pairings the child grimaces at the chime alone. A teacher gives a sticker for every correct answer at first, then switches to rewarding correct answers only now and then.

In another program, a therapist praises a nail-biting client for progress, and separately removes an annoying alarm as soon as the client completes a task. A parent notes that a toddler learns to say please more often after watching an older sibling get treats for saying it.

questions.stem: The child grimaces at the chime alone after it repeatedly precedes bitter syrup. In classical conditioning terms, the chime has become which of the following?
questions.explain: Through pairing with the bitter syrup, the unconditioned stimulus, the previously neutral chime becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers the grimace.

questions.stem: The teacher switches from a sticker for every correct answer to rewarding correct answers only occasionally and unpredictably. This unpredictable schedule tends to produce which outcome?
choices: High, steady responding that resists extinction
Responding only right after each reward
No change compared with rewarding every answer
questions.explain: A variable-ratio schedule produces high, steady response rates that are especially resistant to extinction, which is why occasional unpredictable rewards are powerful.

questions.stem: The therapist removes an annoying alarm as soon as the client finishes a task, and task completion rises. Removing the alarm is an example of which of the following?
questions.explain: Negative reinforcement increases a behavior by removing an unpleasant stimulus, here the alarm, when the desired behavior occurs.

questions.stem: Praising the client for reducing nail-biting, which then decreases nail-biting further, uses praise as which of the following?
choices: A positive reinforcer for the competing behavior
questions.explain: Praise here is a positive reinforcer that strengthens the desired behavior by adding a pleasant consequence.

questions.stem: The toddler says please more often after seeing an older sibling rewarded for saying it. This best illustrates which of the following?
questions.explain: Learning by watching another person be rewarded is observational learning driven by vicarious reinforcement, as described by Bandura.

questions.stem: A dog that once barked at every passing train gradually stops reacting to the harmless, repeated sound, with no reward involved. This decline in response to a repeated, meaningless stimulus is best called which of the following?
questions.explain: Habituation is a decrease in responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus and does not require any prior conditioned association, unlike extinction.

passages.label: Development study
paragraphs: A longitudinal study follows people from childhood into adulthood and records how they resolve life challenges. A teenager tries out different clubs, majors, and friend groups while asking who she really is. A toddler in the same study explores freely when a caregiver is reliably present and grows anxious when the caregiver is unpredictable.

Researchers also present moral dilemmas. A young child says stealing is wrong because you might get caught and punished. An adult says a law can be unjust and that broader ethical principles can outweigh it. Over the years, the team also tracks how each participant describes the self and how confident each feels about specific tasks.

questions.stem: The teenager who tries out many clubs and roles while asking who she is fits which of Erikson's stages?
questions.explain: Adolescence centers on the identity versus role confusion stage, in which a person explores roles to form a coherent sense of self.

questions.stem: The young child who says stealing is wrong only because you might be punished is reasoning at which level of moral development?
questions.explain: Preconventional moral reasoning focuses on avoiding punishment and gaining rewards, not on social approval or abstract principles.

questions.stem: The adult who argues that an unjust law can be outweighed by broader ethical principles is reasoning at which level?
questions.explain: Postconventional reasoning appeals to abstract principles and universal ethics that can override specific laws.

questions.stem: In Erikson's framework, the toddler who explores confidently only when the caregiver is reliably present is working through which stage?
questions.explain: The earliest Eriksonian stage, trust versus mistrust, concerns whether a dependable caregiver leads the infant to view the world as safe.

questions.stem: Researchers note that young children describe themselves mostly by concrete features like hair color, while adolescents describe themselves using abstract traits and beliefs. This shift best reflects which of the following?
choices: A steady decline in self-esteem with age
The development of a more abstract self-concept
questions.explain: As cognition matures, the self-concept moves from concrete physical descriptions toward abstract psychological traits and values.

questions.stem: A participant is very confident she can pass a specific chemistry exam if she studies, though her overall sense of self-worth is only average. Her exam confidence is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Self-efficacy is the belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task, which can be high even when general self-esteem is only moderate.

passages.label: Attribution survey
paragraphs: A social psychology study examines how people explain behavior. Participants read about a driver who cuts off another car and about a student who fails a test. They also rate their own successes and failures, and complete measures of beliefs and feelings toward unfamiliar groups.

Most participants say the rude driver is simply a bad person, while explaining their own rude driving as caused by being in a rush. They credit their own good grades to ability but blame bad grades on unfair tests. In a separate task, teachers who are told that certain randomly chosen students are gifted later rate those students as higher achievers, and those students improve.

questions.stem: Participants call the rude driver a bad person while blaming their own rude driving on being rushed. Their judgment of the other driver reflects which of the following?
questions.explain: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overweight personal, dispositional causes and underweight situational causes when explaining others' behavior.

questions.stem: The contrast between blaming the other driver's character but blaming the situation for one's own identical behavior is best labeled as which of the following?
questions.explain: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute others' actions to disposition while attributing our own to the situation.

questions.stem: Participants credit their good grades to ability but blame bad grades on unfair tests. This pattern is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: The self-serving bias protects self-esteem by attributing successes to internal factors and failures to external ones.

questions.stem: Teachers told that random students are gifted later rate them as higher achievers, and those students improve. This outcome best illustrates which of the following?
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an initially false expectation changes behavior in ways that make the expectation come true.

questions.stem: A participant believes an unfamiliar group is lazy, dislikes them, and refuses to hire them. The refusal to hire is best classified as which of the following?
questions.explain: Discrimination is the behavioral component, unequal treatment based on group membership, distinct from the cognitive stereotype and the affective prejudice.

questions.stem: Reminding students of a negative stereotype about their group right before a test lowers their scores, even though nothing about the test changed. This effect is best described as which of the following?
choices: A self-fulfilling prophecy created by the teacher
questions.explain: Stereotype threat is the drop in performance that arises when people fear confirming a negative stereotype about their own group.

passages.label: Hospital roles
paragraphs: A sociologist observes a busy teaching hospital. A resident is a physician to patients, a student to attending doctors, and a mentor to nurses in training, and she sometimes struggles to meet all of these expectations at once. Staff behave formally and reassuringly at the bedside but joke and vent in the break room.

The sociologist notes that some positions, like being born into a wealthy family, are assigned at birth, while others, like becoming a lead surgeon, are earned. A new nurse carefully manages how he dresses and speaks to appear competent to patients and supervisors.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, Ch. 4 (Society and Social Interaction)

questions.stem: The resident struggles to satisfy the different demands of being a physician, a student, and a mentor at the same time. This clash between the expectations of her different statuses is best called which of the following?
questions.explain: Role conflict arises from incompatible demands of two or more different statuses a person holds at once, unlike role strain, which comes from a single role.

questions.stem: Suppose instead the resident feels torn by competing demands within the single role of physician, such as being both efficient and caring. This tension within one role is best labeled as which of the following?
questions.explain: Role strain is the tension among the various demands of a single role, whereas role conflict is between separate roles.

questions.stem: Staff act formal and reassuring at the bedside but joke and vent in the break room. In Goffman's dramaturgical approach, the break room functions as which of the following?
questions.explain: In dramaturgical analysis, the back stage is where people relax and drop the managed performance they present on the front stage.

questions.stem: The new nurse carefully manages his dress and speech to appear competent to patients and supervisors. This effort is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Impression management is the process of controlling how one presents oneself in order to shape others' perceptions.

questions.stem: Being born into a wealthy family versus becoming a lead surgeon illustrates the difference between which pair?
questions.explain: An ascribed status is assigned without effort, such as by birth, while an achieved status is earned through one's actions.

questions.stem: For one physician, being a famous surgeon overshadows all her other statuses in how others treat her. A status that dominates others in this way is best called which of the following?
questions.explain: A master status is the status that dominates how a person is perceived and organizes their social identity above their other statuses.

passages.label: Paradigms on schooling
paragraphs: A sociology seminar asks students to explain public schooling using different theoretical lenses. One student argues that schools exist because they perform useful functions for society, such as teaching skills and sorting people into jobs. Another argues that schools mainly reproduce the advantages of wealthy families and keep power unequal.

A third student focuses on the small-scale meanings created in classrooms, such as how a label like troublemaker shapes a student's self-image and behavior. The seminar also notes that openly socializing children is a benefit everyone recognizes, while keeping young people out of the job market is a less obvious effect.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, Ch. 1 (An Introduction to Sociology)

questions.stem: The student who says schools exist because they perform useful functions like teaching skills and sorting workers is using which theoretical approach?
questions.explain: Structural functionalism explains social institutions by the functions they perform to maintain the stability of society as a whole.

questions.stem: The student who argues that schools mainly reproduce the advantages of the wealthy and preserve unequal power is using which approach?
questions.explain: Conflict theory, rooted in Marx, emphasizes how institutions maintain inequality and serve the interests of powerful groups.

questions.stem: The student focused on how a label like troublemaker shapes a student's self-image in everyday classroom interactions is using which approach?
questions.explain: Symbolic interactionism is a micro-level approach that studies how people create and respond to shared meanings and labels in interaction.

questions.stem: Openly socializing children is a benefit everyone recognizes, while keeping young people out of the job market is a hidden effect. These two are best described as which pair?
questions.explain: A manifest function is an intended, recognized consequence, while a latent function is an unintended, less obvious one.

questions.stem: Which pair of approaches is best matched to a macro-level, large-scale analysis of schooling rather than a micro-level one?
questions.explain: Functionalism and conflict theory are macro-level paradigms that analyze large social structures, while symbolic interactionism is micro-level.

questions.stem: A researcher predicts that unequal school funding will widen the gap between rich and poor neighborhoods over time. This prediction follows most directly from which approach?
questions.explain: Conflict theory predicts that institutional arrangements like unequal funding will reproduce and deepen social inequality.

passages.label: Country dataset
paragraphs: A demographer compares two countries. Country A has high birth rates and high death rates and a young population. Country B has low birth rates, low death rates, and a growing share of older adults. Over 50 years, Country A's death rate falls sharply due to better sanitation while births stay high, and its population surges.

The demographer also studies movement of people. Many young workers leave rural areas of Country A because there are few jobs, and they move to cities in Country B that offer employment. Some analysts warn that population may outgrow the food supply, while others point to new farming technology as a solution.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, Ch. 20 (Population, Urbanization, and the Environment)

questions.stem: Country A's death rate falls sharply while birth rates stay high, causing its population to surge. This pattern is characteristic of which of the following?
choices: The final stage of the demographic transition
An early stage of the demographic transition
questions.explain: In an early transition stage, death rates drop due to improvements like sanitation while birth rates remain high, producing rapid population growth.

questions.stem: Country B has low birth and death rates and a rising share of older adults. A useful tool for displaying this age-and-sex structure is which of the following?
questions.explain: A population pyramid displays the distribution of a population by age and sex, revealing patterns such as an aging society.

questions.stem: Young workers leave rural Country A because of scarce jobs and move to cities in Country B that offer work. The scarce jobs at home are best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from an origin, such as a lack of jobs, while pull factors attract them to a destination.

questions.stem: The analysts who warn that population may outgrow the food supply are drawing on which perspective?
questions.explain: Malthusian theory warns that population, growing geometrically, can outpace food production, which grows more slowly.

questions.stem: The large-scale movement of people from the countryside into the cities of Country B is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Urbanization is the growing concentration of a population in cities, often driven by rural-to-urban migration for work.

questions.stem: The analysts who respond that new farming technology can keep pace with population growth best represent which view?
choices: The first stage of the demographic transition
questions.explain: The cornucopian view holds that human innovation and technology will continue to solve resource limits as population grows.

passages.label: Mobility study
paragraphs: A sociologist studies how people move up or down the social ladder. In one country, a person's position is fixed at birth by the family they are born into and cannot change, no matter their effort. In another, people can move between levels based on education and work, though family background still shapes their chances.

The study finds that children of college-educated parents are far more likely to attend college themselves, partly because they grow up with books, museum visits, and comfort navigating institutions. Many people nonetheless believe that anyone who works hard can get ahead. In one family, the children become professionals while their parents worked in manual jobs.
passages.source_ref: OpenStax Introduction to Sociology 3e, Ch. 9 (Social Stratification in the United States)

questions.stem: The country where a person's position is fixed at birth and cannot change describes which type of stratification system?
questions.explain: A caste system fixes status at birth with no legitimate mobility, unlike an open class system where movement is possible.

questions.stem: Children of college-educated parents grow up with books, museum visits, and ease navigating institutions, which later helps them succeed. These advantages are best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Cultural capital refers to non-financial assets such as knowledge, tastes, and skills that help people succeed within social institutions.

questions.stem: Many people believe anyone who works hard can get ahead, even though family background strongly shapes outcomes. This belief system is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: The ideology of meritocracy holds that rewards flow from individual effort and talent, which can obscure the structural advantages of birth.

questions.stem: In one family, the children become professionals while their parents worked in manual jobs. This rise in position from parents to children is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Intergenerational mobility is a change in social position from one generation to the next, such as children reaching a higher class than their parents.

questions.stem: A functionalist argues that societies pay surgeons more than clerks because such important, hard-to-fill jobs must attract talented people. This argument is known as which of the following?
questions.explain: The Davis-Moore thesis is the functionalist claim that stratification is useful because greater rewards motivate the most qualified people to fill the most important positions.

questions.stem: During a technology boom, a whole cohort of workers moves into higher-paying jobs as the economy adds many new positions. This upward movement of many people due to changes in the economy is best described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Structural mobility is movement of many people up or down the ladder caused by changes in the wider economy rather than by individual effort alone.
